item.title: Justice Dept. Dismisses Threats Case in Minnesota Days Before Trial
item.description: The government said it could not prove that a man accused of threatening federal agents had committed a crime, adding to the scores of cases in the administration’s deportation efforts that have unraveled.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto Londoño
item.media:credit: Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times
item.media:description: On Jan. 14, after a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot a Venezuelan migrant following a high-speed chase in Minneapolis, protesters broke into a couple of vehicles that belonged to F.B.I. agents.

item.title: Colorado Was Targeted as Trump Fumed Over Election Denier, Email Shows
item.description: The state has accused the government in a lawsuit of retaliating after the conviction of Tina Peters, a Trump supporter. An administration official convened a group to discuss “immediate actions.”
item.dc:creator: Reis Thebault
item.media:credit: Larry Robinson/The Grand Junction Daily Sentinel, via Associated Press
item.media:description: Tina Peters, the former Mesa County clerk and recorder, in court in Grand Junction, Colo., in 2024.

item.title: Series of Michigan Shootings Leave 6 Dead, Including Gunman
item.description: The gunman, Chad Hickman, was found dead in a wooded area near Whitlock Lake in Caldwell Township, the authorities said. A motive for the shootings was not immediately known.
item.dc:creator: Mark Walker

item.title: Man, 18, Pleads Guilty to Repeatedly Kicking Sea Lion in California
item.description: The man bobbed and wove before lobbing a kick at a sea lion in San Diego last month, a video of the episode shows.
item.dc:creator: Ishani Desai
item.media:credit: Mario Tama/Getty Images
item.media:description: Sea lions at La Jolla cove in San Diego. An 18-year-old man pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal charges of assaulting a sea lion last month.

item.title: South Florida Venue Cancels Rally With a Pro-Palestinian Congresswoman
item.description: Representative Rashida Tlaib was supposed to headline an event called “Chomp the Oligarchy” for three candidates for Congress who face Jewish Democrats in Tuesday’s primary.
item.dc:creator: Tim Balk
item.media:credit: Eric Lee for The New York Times
item.media:description: Representative Rashida Tlaib, Democrat of Michigan, has drawn criticism, and a 2023 censure in Congress, for embracing a pro-Palestinian slogan that many Jews consider a call for the eradication of Israel.

item.title: Two Billy Goats Boarded a Bus in Portland. They Did Not Have Passes.
item.description: Security camera footage showed the goats entering the TriMet bus in Portland, Ore., through the middle doors before some passengers shooed them off. They have since been reunited with their owner.
item.dc:creator: Neil Vigdor

item.title: President Trump Takes Credit for Steep Crime Rate Declines
item.description: Violent crime rates, including murder, have dropped precipitously. The trend began before the president’s current term.
item.dc:creator: Shaila Dewan and Karoun Demirjian
item.media:credit: Al Drago for The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump at an event in Garden City, N.Y., on Long Island on Friday.

item.title: John Carro, Jurist Who Had Early Brush With Lee Harvey Oswald, Dies at 98
item.description: Decades before his rise to the New York State appellate court, he was a probation officer who tried to help Mr. Oswald, then a teenager living in the Bronx.
item.dc:creator: Richard Sandomir
item.media:credit: Lee Romero/The New York Times
item.media:description: John Carro in 1998. Before he became a lawyer, he was a police office, a social worker and a mayoral aide.

item.title: The 5 Congress Members Whose Families Trade the Most Stocks
item.description: Some lawmakers and their families have traded millions of dollars worth of stocks since the start of this term.
item.dc:creator: Olivia Diaz
item.media:credit: Jeenah Moon/Reuters
item.media:description: A law passed in 2012, the STOCK Act, emphasizes that insider trading is illegal among lawmakers, as it is for the general public, and requires them to periodically disclose trades of shares held by them and members of their families.

item.title: Stock Trading in Congress Becomes an Attack Line in Midterm Campaigns
item.description: Republican and Democratic challengers are both using the issue to attack members of Congress as unethical, seizing on a common practice that enrages voters.
item.dc:creator: Annie Karni
item.media:credit: Angela Weiss/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Almost 60 percent of lawmakers in Congress own stock, according to an analysis by Common Cause, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization focused on making government more accountable.

item.title: Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola Pushes Back Against Endorsement From Kamala Harris
item.description: The campaign of Mary Peltola said it was focused on issues important to Alaska and did not approve a message of support from Ms. Harris.
item.dc:creator: Tim Balk
item.media:credit: Kerry Tasker/Reuters; Philip Cheung for The New York Times
item.media:description: Former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska did not appear to be happy that former Vice President Kamala Harris put out a fund-raising appeal on her behalf. Ms. Harris lost the 2024 presidential election in Alaska by 14 points.

item.title: Lawsuit Accuses Selena Gomez of Defrauding Investors in Mental Health Site
item.description: The actor, singer and beauty mogul founded Wondermind, a mental health platform, with her mother. Investors put in more than $1 million in the venture, which “quietly collapsed,” the suit said.
item.dc:creator: Remy Tumin
item.media:credit: Jack Plunkett/Invision, via Associated Press
item.media:description: Selena Gomez and her mother, Mandy Teefey, at a panel focused on mental health during the SXSW conference in Austin, Texas, in 2024.

item.dc:creator: Karoun Demirjian
item.media:credit: John Mcdonnell/Associated Press
item.media:description: National Guard troops patrol the World War II Memorial on Friday after it was vandalized.

item.title: Mary Morello, Free Speech Activist Who Defended Explicit Lyrics, Dies at 102
item.description: An Illinois teacher — and the mother of the rock star Tom Morello — she took on Tipper Gore during culture war skirmishes over warning labels on records.
item.dc:creator: Alex Williams
item.media:credit: Kevin Winter/Getty Images
item.media:description: Mary Morello in 2016. She was in her mid-60s when, with a nudge from her rocker son, she retired from teaching to found Parents for Rock and Rap in 1987.

item.title: She Sewed the Blue Angels’ Suits for 40 Years. Then a Big Company Got the Job.
item.description: Jellie Whitehurst in Pensacola, Fla., was surprised to learn that after decades, the Navy had awarded a $1.7 million contract to a company in Virginia to supply the gear.

item.media:credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect

item.title: Russell Fry Backs Darline Graham in South Carolina Senate Runoff Amid Trump Pressure

item.title: Brad Pitt’s Return to Drinking Is Not Unsafe, Experts Say
item.description: His disclosure in an interview revived a key question about sobriety: whether someone who once drank dangerously can ever drink moderately.
item.dc:creator: Mark Walker
item.media:credit: Angela Weiss/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Brad Pitt last year. “I had taken things as far as I could take it, so I removed my drinking privileges,” he told The New York Times in 2019.

item.title: Why the D.O.J. Is Pursuing Low-Level Fraud Cases

item.title: Trump’s Justice Dept. Targets Smaller Fraud Cases
item.description: As the Trump administration drops charges against corporations and the wealthy, it is also taking aim at small-scale fraud cases, including against the operator of a weathered food truck in California.
item.dc:creator: Devlin Barrett
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: Justice Department officials have internally declared that each assistant U.S. attorney should have at least 25 open cases at all times.

item.title: Is Activism Hurting Sociology? Sociologists Are Torn.
item.description: A group of sociologists broke away in protest from their colleagues over disagreements about Israel. Some worry the political stances are harming the field.
item.dc:creator: Vimal Patel
item.media:credit: Jackie Molloy for The New York Times
item.media:description: Attendees of a breakaway sociology conference in New York on Tuesday made signs in support of Palestine.

item.title: ‘A Dying Community’: An Energy Crisis Worsened by the War Strains Alaska
item.description: Diesel generators produce the electricity for small towns and hamlets like Manley Hot Springs, Alaska. Prices are soaring with no end in sight.
item.dc:creator: Anna Griffin and Ruth Fremson
item.category: US and Israeli Attack on Iran (2026)
item.media:description: Alaskans in remote villages are “having to choose between feeding their families and having a warm home.”

item.title: Inside Rural Alaska’s Energy Crisis
item.description: Anna Griffin, our Pacific Northwest bureau chief, visits rural Alaska to look at the ways the Iran war worsened an energy crisis there.
